title: Add inline code examples in data processing module docstrings
body:
As first discussed in [this comment](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/1666#issuecomment-993962742), module docstrings  should contain inline code examples to show a working example of the module with the correct syntax without needing to find an example page.

To prevent example functions from being run in tests, add `_doctest_skip__ = [MODULE NAME]` under the import statements.

title: Subset grid using a geopandas.GeoDataFrame polygon with grdcut -F
body:
**Description of the desired feature**

Spatial subsetting/cropping/masking/clipping of a raster grid using a polygon (stored in an ESRI shapefile or [`geopandas.GeoDataFrame`](https://geopandas.org/docs/reference/api/geopandas.GeoDataFrame.html#geopandas.GeoDataFrame)) is a common operation, e.g. to extract a Region of Interest.

<!-- Please be as detailed as you can in your description. If possible, include an example of how you would like to use this feature (even better if it's a code example). -->

Currently, the [`pygmt.grdcut`](https://www.pygmt.org/v0.4.1/api/generated/pygmt.grdcut.html) function in PyGMT v0.4.1 (added in #492) can do bounding box (via 'region' `-R`), circular (via 'circ_subregion' `-S`) and z-value (via 'z_subregion' `-Z`) based subsetting.

It would be nice to add in the [`grdcut -F`](https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/latest/grdcut.html#f) option too which does polygon-based crops using an ASCII file. Furthermore, it would be even nicer to perform the crop using an in-memory `geopandas.GeoDataFrame` or `shapely.geometry` polygon object!

Technically, this is reinventing the wheel, because there are a few Python libraries that already do this:
- https://corteva.github.io/rioxarray/stable/examples/clip_geom.html
- https://rasterio.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/masking-by-shapefile.html#masking-a-raster-using-a-shapefile
- https://geosynopsis.github.io/xgeo/docs/html/examples.html#subset-data (not very maintained)

But who says the wheel can't be reinvented :smile:

**Are you willing to help implement and maintain this feature?** A bit low on my priority list, but anyone interested is welcome to try.

Steps to implement:
- [ ] Alias the `-F` parameter in grdcut to "polygon" (or another name) at https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/bafb8ab906aa87eb1dab3ce286b9baa91e145099/pygmt/src/grdcut.py#L17-L18
- [ ] Implement the GeoDataFrame -> ASCII file conversion that can be read by `gmt grdcut -F`, may need to use [`tempfile_from_geojson`](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/a0286345933c1eaf2e1fb215809e33f2a792be0b/pygmt/helpers/tempfile.py#L111) or some alternative way.
- [ ] Add a gallery example for this to https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/tree/main/examples/gallery/images

title: Better support for plotting text in 3D at different heights
body:
**Description of the desired feature**

For 3D plots, it should be possible to plot text at different heights based on a 'z' column, see https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/6.2/text.html#z. The current implementation of `text` in PyGMT (see https://www.pygmt.org/v0.4.0/api/generated/pygmt.Figure.text.html) does support this, but users have to provide the xyz input into the `textfiles` parameter, and it is also not very discoverable for new users.

<!-- Please be as detailed as you can in your description. If possible, include an example of how you would like to use this feature (even better if it's a code example). -->

It would be nice to have a `z` parameter (in addition to `x` and `y`) to be clear that `text` does support multi-height plotting. Here's a checklist for anyone wanting to work on this 'enhancement'.

TODO:
1. Alias the [`-Z`](https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/6.2/text.html#z), call it `zvalue` (as in `plot3d`)?
2. Add the `z` parameter here:
    https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/945bbc57ffc89a7c29384df48a653295b3f1a435/pygmt/src/text.py#L48-L49
3. Modify the code here to mention that x/y/z triples are also possible (~~need to wait for #1121 though~~ edit: done!):
    https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/945bbc57ffc89a7c29384df48a653295b3f1a435/pygmt/src/text.py#L160-L170
4. Update the `text` API docstring to document the new behaviour.
5. (Optional) Update the tutorial at https://www.pygmt.org/v0.4.0/tutorials/text.html to mention that z-value inputs are supported too.

**Are you willing to help implement and maintain this feature?** Please wait for #1121 before starting work on this (Edit: that PR is merged, so ready to start)!

title: Expand pygmt subplot's documentation for the figsize and subsize parameters
body:
**Description of the desired feature**

The docstring for [pygmt.subplot](https://www.pygmt.org/v0.4.0/api/generated/pygmt.Figure.subplot.html)'s `figsize` (-Ff) and `subsize` (-Fs) parameters are rather brief, and we should expand it to be longer following upstream GMT at https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/6.2/subplot.html#required-arguments-begin-mode. This is a follow up to #822.

<!-- Please be as detailed as you can in your description. If possible, include an example of how you would like to use this feature (even better if it's a code example). -->

## Current state :memo:

https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/d90b3fc889b53633deab6b4ab77612ac7a247c1b/pygmt/src/subplot.py#L56-L61

## Desired state :sparkles:

>     figsize : tuple
>         Specify the final figure dimensions as (*width*, *height*). The subplot
>         dimensions are then calculated from the figure dimensions after
>         accounting for the space that optional tick marks, annotations, labels,
>         and margins occupy between subplots. As for other figures, annotations,
>         ticks, and labels along the outside perimeter are not counted as part
>         of the figure dimensions. To specify different subplot dimensions for
>         each row (or column), append **+f** followed by a comma-separated list
>         of width fractions, a slash, and then the list of height fractions. For
>         example ``figsize="10c/10c+f3,1/1,2"`` will make the first column three
>         times as wide as the second, while the second row will be twice as tall
>         as the first row. A single number means constant widths (or heights)
>         [Default].
>     
>     subsize : tuple
>         Specify the dimensions of each subplot directly as (*width*, *height*).
>         Then, the figure dimensions are computed from the subplot dimensions
>         after adding the space that optional tick marks, annotations, labels,
>         and margins occupy between subplots. As for other figures, annotations,
>         ticks, and labels along the outside perimeter are not counted as part
>         of the figure dimensions. To specify different subplot dimensions for
>         each row (or column), append a comma-separated list of widths, a slash,
>         and then the comma-separated list of heights. A single number means
>         constant widths (or heights) [Default]. For example
>         ``subsize="5c,8c/8c"`` will make the first column 5 cm wide and the
>         second column 8 cm wide, with all having a constant height of 8 cm. The
>         number of values must either be one (constant across the rows or
>         columns) or exactly match the number of rows (or columns). For
>         geographic maps, the height of each subplot depends on your map region
>         and projection. There are two options:
> 
>         1. Specify both ``region`` and ``projection`` and we use these to
>            compute the height of each subplot. All subplots must share the same
>            region and projection and you specify a zero *height*, or
>         2. Select *height* based on trial and error to suit your plot layout.
>     
>         Optionally, you may draw the outline (**+p**\ *pen*) or paint
>         (**+g**\ *fill*\) the figure rectangle behind the subplots, add
>         dividing lines between panels (**+w**\ *pen*), and even expand it via
>         **+c**. These are most useful if you supply **frame="+n"** to
>         ``subplot``, meaning no ticks or annotations will take place in the
>         subplots. By default (**+af**), we auto-scale the fonts and pens based
>         on the geometric mean dimension of the entire figure. Append **+as** to
>         instead determine the scaling from the geometric mean subplot
>         dimension.


## How to make the change :monocle_face:

1. First, read up our contributing guidelines at https://www.pygmt.org/v0.4.0/contributing.html#editing-the-documentation
2. Leave a comment below, stating that you will tackle this issue. We will assign you to this issue and you can then start working on it.
3. To edit the `subplot` module's docstring, go to https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/edit/master/pygmt/src/subplot.py and add in the new docstring!
4. Submit a pull request, and be sure to fill it up with as much detail as possible.

:partying_face: Good luck, and let us know if you need any help :)

**Are you willing to help implement and maintain this feature?** Happy to review someone's Pull Request on it.

title: `sequence_join` treats any string containing a space as a datetime (crashes `labels=` in `magnetic_rose`/`directional_rose`)
body:
Hi, thanks for maintaining PyGMT. In `pygmt/helpers/utils.py`, `sequence_join` detects datetime-like items with

```python
elif " " in str(item):
    _values.append(np.datetime_as_string(np.asarray(item, dtype="datetime64")))
```

A space is normal in label text and does not mean the item is temporal. With the pinned source and NumPy 2.x:

```
sequence_join(["W", "E", "S", "N"], sep=",", size=4)          -> 'W,E,S,N'
sequence_join(["W", "E", "S", "Pole Nord"], sep=",", size=4)  -> ValueError: Cannot create a NumPy datetime other than NaT with generic units
```

`pygmt/alias.py` calls `sequence_join` for every non-string iterable whenever `sep` is set. `magnetic_rose` and `directional_rose` build `Alias(labels, name="labels", prefix="+l", sep=",", size=4)` and document `labels` as free text. So a label with a space crashes before GMT is even called. (`magnetic_rose` already escapes spaces in the scalar `declination_label` as `\040`, which suggests labels with spaces are expected.)

A type check, e.g. `isinstance(item, (datetime.datetime, datetime.date, np.datetime64)) or hasattr(item, "isoformat")`, instead of sniffing for a space would fix it. Plain strings could then go through `str(item)`, with the same `\040` escaping if GMT needs it.

I found this while testing [physverify](https://github.com/rcgiri-physics/physverify), a small verification tool I'm working on, against public codes. The tests and this write-up were done with help from an AI assistant; the numbers come from actually running the code.

comments.body:
👋 Thanks for opening your first issue here!

Please make sure you filled out the template with as much detail as possible. You might also want to take a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [code of conduct](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/.github/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

Thanks for the report, @rcgiri-physics.

### Background 

```python
elif " " in str(item):
    _values.append(np.datetime_as_string(np.asarray(item, dtype="datetime64")))
```

Some background: the code above was added in #4097 and later modified in #4358. It was originally copied from the `kwargs_to_strings` decorator ([decorators.py#L751-L759](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/e96f272ebfcc71b12298b8b9ad1914ef747c1be5/pygmt/helpers/decorators.py#L751-L759)):

The intent was to let users pass datetime-like objects (e.g., `datetime.datetime`, `pd.Timestamp`) to parameters like `region`, because `str()` of these objects contains a space (`2010-01-01 00:00:00`), which GMT can't parse.

### Limitations of the current implementation

The current implementation has two side effects:

1. Any string containing a space is treated as a datetime, so a normal text label crashes:
   ```python
   >>> sequence_join(["W", "E", "S", "Pole Nord"], sep=",", size=4)
   ValueError: Cannot create a NumPy datetime other than NaT with generic units
   ```
   This affects every parameter that takes free text, including `labels` in `magnetic_rose`/`directional_rose` and `alabel`/`blabel`/`clabel` in `ternary` (e.g., `alabel="Clay A"`).
2. Datetime-like strings with a space are rewritten in ISO 8601 format, e.g., `sequence_join(["2010-01-01 01:01", "2010-01-02 01:01"])` gives `2010-01-01T01:01/2010-01-02T01:01`. For `region` this is actually what we want, because GMT can't parse a space in a datetime:
   ```
   $ gmt basemap -R"2010-01-01 01:01/2010-01-02 01:01/0/1" -JX10c/5c -Baf -pdf map
   basemap [ERROR]: Could not parse 2010-01-01 01:01 into Geographical, Cartesian, or Temporal coordinates!
   $ gmt makecpt -Cgray -T"2010-01-01 01:01/2010-01-03 01:01/1d"
   makecpt [ERROR]: Option T: Unable to parse min value from 2010-01-01 01:01
   ```
   For other parameters, however, users may want to typeset the string literally even though the strings are datetime-like.

#4961 replaces the space check with a type check. That fixes item 1 but breaks code like `region=["2010-01-01 01:01", "2010-01-02 01:01", 0, 1]`, which works now.

The underlying problem is that we can't tell from the value alone whether `"2010-01-01 01:01"` is a datetime or a literal string. Only the parameter can tell us. As far as I know, only a few GMT options accept datetimes: 

- the common `-R` option (`region` in PyGMT)
- the `-T` option of `grd2cpt`/`makecpt`/`histogram` (`series` in PyGMT, which will be migrated to the alias system later).


### Proposed changes

So I propose adding a boolean parameter (e.g., `datetime` or `datetime_like`) to `sequence_join` and `Alias`:

- `False` (default): no conversion at all; every item is converted with `str()`. Free-text parameters are safe by default.
- `True`: datetime-like objects are converted to ISO 8601 strings, and strings containing a space are parsed as datetimes (passed through unchanged if parsing fails, so GMT reports the error). This would be manually enabled only for `region` and `series`, and more parameters if necessary.

@GenericMappingTools/pygmt-maintainers Any comments?

title: Add the Perspective class for setting perspective view
body:
GMT’s `-p` option enables perspective view by setting the azimuth and elevation of the viewpoint. The full documentation is available at:
[https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/6.6/gmt.html#perspective-full](https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/6.6/gmt.html#perspective-full)

The GMT command-line syntax is rather complex:

```bash
-p[x|y|z]azim[/elev[/zlevel]][+wlon0/lat0[/z0]][+vx0/y0]
```

At present, we must pass the raw string directly to the `perspective` parameter in the first plotting command, and then specify `perspective=True` in subsequent commands. This approach feels un-Pythonic.

One possible improvement is to define an auxiliary class that can be passed to the `perspective` parameter, for example:

```python
perspective = Perspective(azimuth, elevation, zlevel, ...)
```

However, a more Pythonic design might be to provide a method—similar to Matplotlib’s [`[view_init](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/mpl_toolkits.mplot3d.axes3d.Axes3D.view_init.html)`](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/mpl_toolkits.mplot3d.axes3d.Axes3D.view_init.html)—that allows setting the perspective once and reusing it, like so:

```python
import pygmt

fig = pygmt.Figure()
fig.set_perspective(azimuth=xxx, elevation=xxx, zlevel=xxx)
fig.basemap(region=xxx, projection=xxx, perspective=True)
fig.coast(..., perspective=True)
fig.text(...)  # No perspective parameter needed
```

With this approach, the `perspective` parameter can simply take a boolean value—`True` to apply the perspective settings defined by `fig.set_perspective`, and `False` to disable them. This would also simplify the docstring for the `perspective` parameter.

This is still an early idea, and I’d appreciate any feedback before proceeding with implementation.

comments.body:
I'm ok with a `pygmt.param.Perspective` class, but slightly against implementing `fig.set_perspective`, mostly because unlike `fig.set_panel`, there's no easy way to translate that to GMT syntax. We would still have to support the old method of passing `perspective` through e.g. `basemap` on the first call, and having the new `set_perspective` method would go against the 'There should be one-- and preferably only one --obvious way to do it'. It is possible to switch to the new syntax only, but then there would be a tricky deprecation cycle.

Implementation-wise, it might require https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/2388 (make PyGMT stateful), at least having state in the `Figure` class instance.

Personally, I would encourage a syntax that's more like:

```python
import pygmt

fig = pygmt.Figure()
pp = pygmt.param.Perspective(azimuth=xxx, elevation=xxx, zlevel=xxx)
fig.basemap(region=xxx, projection=xxx, perspective=pp)
fig.coast(..., perspective=pp)  # can also use perspective=True
fig.text(...)  # No perspective parameter needed
```

this same style of instantiating a param class first, and then using it in the Figure methods can be learned more easily across the different Alias classes (Box/Pattern/Pen/Projection/etc) that are tracked in #4122.

OK. I've implemented a `Perspective` class in PR #4201. The implementation is simple, and we need to choose suitable parameter names.


`-p[x|y|z]azim[/elev[/zlevel]][+wlon0/lat0[/z0]][+vx0/y0]`:

- [x] `x|y|z`: `plane` #4201 
- [x] `azim`: `azimuth` #4201 
- [x] `elev`: `elevation` #4201 
- [x] `zlevel`: `level` #4201 
- [ ] `+w`: `center` [GMT uses `world`]
- [ ] `+v`: `viewpoint` [GMT uses `view`]

Reference:

- GMT documentation: https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/6.6/gmt.html#perspective-full
- GMT long option: https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/gmt/blob/41423e5200fc2d5e83043f6a5df4b18d29e9a165/src/gmt_common_longoptions.h#L151

Currently, the `perspective` parameter supports the following input forms:

- A single value: *azimuth*
- A sequence of two values: (*azimuth*, *elevation*)
- A sequence of three values: (*azimuth*, *elevation*, *zlevel*)
- ``True``, to reuse the previous perspective setting
- A string (e.g., "x150/30+w30/30") to use the full GMT `-p` syntax with more controls

Apparently, option 5 is not Pythonic, but it's not commonly used. The `Perspective` class will supersede it once implemented. Even after implementing `Perspective`, for backward compatibility, we still need to support the above forms, and more importantly, `perspective=30` is simpler than `perspective=Perspective(azimuth=30)`. Therefore, the `Perspective` class is not a high-priority feature and does not need to be completed before submitting the paper.

PS: I've started PR #4206 to migrate the `perspective` parameter to the new alias system.

I find the GMT documentation about `+w`/`+v` confusing (https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/6.7/gmt.html#perspective-full): > For frames used for animation, we fix the center of your data domain. Specify another center using one of the following modifiers: > > +w - Project lon0/lat0 (and z0 if applicable) to the center of the page size. > +v - Specify the coordinates of the projected 2-D view point as x0/y0. while the command usage (https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/gmt/blob/cb23d51e997641381b17308f6127a29555b7423e/src/gmt_init.c#L8370-L8377) is clearer: > For a plain rotation about the z-axis, give rotation angle only and optionally use modifiers > +w or +v to select location of axis: > +w Specify a fixed coordinate point [region center]. > +v Set a fixed projected point [panel center]. Here is a script to understand the behavior: ``` gmt begin map gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10c -Ba2g2 gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10 -Ba2g2 -p30 gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10c -Ba2g2 -Xw+5c gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10c -Ba2g2 -p30+w4/4 gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10c -Ba2g2 -p60+w4/4 gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10c -Ba2g2 -p120+w4/4 gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10c -Ba2g2 -Xw+10c gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10c -Ba2g2 -p30+v4/4 gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10c -Ba2g2 -p60+v4/4 gmt basemap -R-10/10/-10/10 -JX10c -Ba2g2 -p120+v4/4 gmt end show ``` As can be seen, `-p` without `+w`/`+v` rotates about the plot origin; `+w4/4` rotates about the user data coordinates (4, 4); `+v4/4` rotates about the plot coordinates ("4c", "4c"). From the [source code](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/gmt/blob/cb23d51e997641381b17308f6127a29555b7423e/src/gmt_init.c#L2803), it's also clear that `+w`/`+v` are exclusive (when used together, `+v` has a higher priority). As mentioned above, GMT recommends long-form names `view`/`world` for `+v`/`+w`, respectively, which I feel difficult to understand. What about using the same terminology as [the `Position` class](https://www.pygmt.org/dev/api/generated/pygmt.params.Position.html#pygmt.params.Position), i.e., - `refpoint`: specify the fixed reference point for the rotation - `cstype`: specify the coordinate system type for the reference point, which can be `mapcoords` and `plotcoords`, e.g., - `refpoint=(4, 4), cstype="mapcoords"` is mapped to `+w4/4` - `refpoint=(4, 4), cstype="plotcoords"` is mapped to `+v4/4`

*Add links to related wrapper discussions, API design threads, or upstream GMT changes here.*

comments.body: There were some discussions in https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/967.

I'm re-reading the discussions in #967. Both #967 and this issue propose supporting ObsPy's `Trace`/`Stream` objects. It sounds like a good idea, but there are still some technical challenges:

1. Some features in the `sac` module require time markers like `T0`-`T9`, which are not available in other data formats (e.g., miniseed). So the available functionality depends on the data format. 
2. Even for `Trace`/`Stream` objects created by reading SAC files, we still need to write them to temporary disk files, because GMT's virtualfile mechanism only supports data tables, grids, and images, not SAC files.

So, I feel we should limit the `Figure.sac` method to SAC files only. We may explore a more general `Figure.waveform` method for plotting `Trace`/`Stream` instead.
I understand. So PR will only complete the warp of the sac first.

title: Improve reporting the GMT version via "pygmt.show_versions()"
body:
Currently, `pygmt.show_versions()` reports the GMT version in two different ways: `version` and `binary version`. In the example below, `version` says `6.7.0`. So one may think GMT 6.7.0 is successfully installed. However, `binary version` says `6.7.0_8931e47_2026.01.12`. This indicates that the installed GMT version is actually GMT 6.6.0 with changes towards 6.7.0 but not the finally released GMT 6.7.0. I feel this can be misleading. In contrast, for PyGMT, we have `v0.20.0.dev62` under `version`. So, it's directly clear that this is v0.19.0 with changes towards v0.20.0 and not the finally released v0.20.0. When running `gmt --version` I get `6.7.0_8931e47_2026.01.12`, which is the same output as listed for `binary version`.

```bash
(pygmt_env_dev) C:\Users\Admin>python -c "import pygmt; pygmt.show_versions()"
PyGMT information:
  version: v0.20.0.dev62
System information:
  python: 3.14.2 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Dec  6 2025, 11:17:27) [MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)]
  executable: C:\ProgramData\Anaconda3\envs\pygmt_env_dev\python.exe
  machine: Windows-10-10.0.19045-SP0
Dependency information:
  numpy: 2.4.1
  pandas: 2.3.3
  xarray: 2025.12.0
  packaging: 25.0
  contextily: 1.7.0
  geopandas: 1.1.2
  IPython: 9.9.0
  pyarrow: 22.0.0
  rioxarray: 0.20.0
  gdal: 3.12.1
  ghostscript: 10.06.0
GMT library information:
  version: 6.7.0
  padding: 2
  share dir: C:/Program Files (x86)/gmt6/share
  plugin dir: C:/ProgramData/Anaconda3/envs/pygmt_env_dev/Library/bin/gmt_plugins
  library path: C:/ProgramData/Anaconda3/envs/pygmt_env_dev/Library/bin/gmt.dll
  cores: 4
  grid layout: rows
  image layout:
  binary version: 6.7.0_8931e47_2026.01.12

(pygmt_env_dev) C:\Users\Admin>gmt --version
6.7.0_8931e47_2026.01.12
```

--- 

Beside this, I personally find it confusing to write `v0.20.0.dev62` for v0.19.0 with changes towards v0.20.0 (or v0.19.1). At the beginning I thought that the latest release is v0.20.0 with 62 changes towards the next release. Thus, I think it would be more intuitive to write `v0.19.0.dev62`. But probably doing it in the current way is the common practice. So better not changing this.

comments.body:
> Beside this, I personally find it confusing to write `v0.20.0.dev62` for v0.19.0 with changes towards v0.20.0 (or v0.19.1). At the beginning I thought that the latest release is v0.20.0 with 62 changes towards the next release. Thus, I think it would be more intuitive to write `v0.19.0.dev62`. But probably doing it in the current way is the common practice. So better not changing this.

`v0.20.0.dev62` means the 62nd development release for v0.20.0, rather than 62 changes since v0.20.0.

We can't change it to something like `v0.19.0.dev62`, as shown below:
```
>>> from packaging.version import Version
>>> Version("0.19.0") > Version("0.19.0.dev62")
True

>>> Version("0.19.0") > Version("0.20.0.dev62")
False
```

> In the example below, `version` says `6.7.0`. So one may think GMT 6.7.0 is successfully installed. However, `binary version` says `6.7.0_8931e47_2026.01.12`. This indicates that the installed GMT version is actually GMT 6.6.0 with changes towards 6.7.0 but not the finally released GMT 6.7.0. I feel this can be misleading.

There are two version strings in GMT, the binary version and the library version. The library version string is obtained from the GMT API function `GMT_Get_Version`, which must be in the *major.minor.patch* form. The binary version comes from `gmt --version`. 

Perhaps we should change "version" to "library version"?

> Perhaps we should change "version" to "library version"?

And maybe we can move `binary version` to the top and `library version` to the end, as I feel `binary version` provides the more complete version information.

Maybe update it to:
```
GMT information:
  version: 6.7.0_8931e47_2026.01.12
  padding: 2
  share dir: C:/Program Files (x86)/gmt6/share
  plugin dir: C:/ProgramData/Anaconda3/envs/pygmt_env_dev/Library/bin/gmt_plugins
  library path: C:/ProgramData/Anaconda3/envs/pygmt_env_dev/Library/bin/gmt.dll
  cores: 4
  grid layout: rows
  image layout:
```
The reasons are:

- Strictly speaking, some information like "share dir" are not information about "GMT library". Changing it to "GMT information" may make more sense
- The binary version string provides more accurate information than the library version string. So just keep one of them.

title: License and Attribution of the PyGMT Logo?
body:
Hello PyGMT Team,

I am the founder of the @localizethedocs organization, and the [pygmt-docs-l10n](https://github.com/localizethedocs/pygmt-docs-l10n) project is now published. The following commands are what I used for generating `.eps` files for each type of logos:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt.git pygmt
cd pygmt
git checkout 3fd34d1afd9efd92d44848e9d320badb7c3ef1b1
conda create --prefix ./.venv --yes
conda env update --file environment.yml --prefix ./.venv
conda activate ./.venv
python -m pip install .
python -c "from pygmt.src.pygmtlogo import _create_logo; _create_logo(theme='light', wordmark='none',       figname='pygmtlogo_light_none.eps')"
python -c "from pygmt.src.pygmtlogo import _create_logo; _create_logo(theme='light', wordmark='horizontal', figname='pygmtlogo_light_horizontal.eps')"
python -c "from pygmt.src.pygmtlogo import _create_logo; _create_logo(theme='dark',  wordmark='none',       figname='pygmtlogo_dark_none.eps')"
python -c "from pygmt.src.pygmtlogo import _create_logo; _create_logo(theme='dark',  wordmark='horizontal', figname='pygmtlogo_dark_horizontal.eps')"
```

Then, I converted them from EPS to SVG by uploading them to the [CloudConvert](https://cloudconvert.com/eps-to-svg) platform.

To place the PyGMT logo at the top of the README, I need to upload the logo to the [localizethedocs/static](https://github.com/localizethedocs/static) repository and then access it via jsDelivr.  Therefore, I would like to confirm the **license** of these logos and what **attribution** is required.

comments.body:
👋 Thanks for opening your first issue here!

Please make sure you filled out the template with as much detail as possible. You might also want to take a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [code of conduct](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/.github/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

Based on the [documentation](https://www.pygmt.org/v0.19.0/gallery/embellishments/pygmtlogo.html), it seems that the current logo was designed by @sfrooti, and it is licensed under the CC BY 4.0 license in the [sfrooti/PyGMT-Logo](https://github.com/sfrooti/PyGMT-Logo) repository. If so, how about the following attribution? Code: ```html logo/pygmt-dark.svg Link By Studio Raada, licensed under CC BY 4.0. logo/pygmt-light.svg Link By Studio Raada, licensed under CC BY 4.0. ``` Preview:

> Based on the [documentation](https://www.pygmt.org/v0.19.0/gallery/embellishments/pygmtlogo.html), it seems that the current logo was designed by [@sfrooti](https://github.com/sfrooti), and it is licensed under the CC BY 4.0 license in the [sfrooti/PyGMT-Logo](https://github.com/sfrooti/PyGMT-Logo) repository.

The original PyGMT logo was designed by @sfrooti and is licensed under CC BY 4.0. The logo was subsequently modified by PyGMT contributors in PR #4616. I guess @sfrooti still owns the copyright if my understanding of CC BY 4.0 is correct.
Hello @seisman, > By Studio Raada, licensed under CC BY 4.0. If so, then is the above attribution acceptable? If not, then what kind of attribution is required?
Ping @GenericMappingTools/pygmt-maintainers for more comments on this topic.

Following https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/deed.en#ref-appropriate-credit, I would say use the name of the creator (Sfurti) rather than the studio name. And since there were modifications made by the PyGMT team, we need to [indicate those changes](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/deed.en#ref-indicate-changes), so maybe something like: ``` By Sfurti, licensed under CC BY 4.0 / Modified from original by the PyGMT Team . ```

> 7\. Following https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/deed.en#ref-appropriate-credit, I would say use the name of the creator (Sfurti) rather than the studio name. And since there were modifications made by the PyGMT team, we need to [indicate those changes](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/deed.en#ref-indicate-changes), so maybe something like: > ``` > By Sfurti, licensed under CC BY 4.0 / Modified from original by the PyGMT Team . > ``` Sounds reasonable. Currently, the [`Figure.pygmtlogo` API documentation](https://www.pygmt.org/dev/api/generated/pygmt.Figure.pygmtlogo.html#pygmt.Figure.pygmtlogo) says: > The design of the logo is kindly provided by [@sfrooti](https://github.com/sfrooti) I think we should also update the docstring to clarify the license.

title: Translate PyGMT documentation into Spanish
body:
**Hi PyGMT team!**

I would like to contribute to the project by **translating the documentation** (starting with the tutorials or quickstart guide) into Spanish. This could help make PyGMT more accessible to students and researchers in Latin America.

Before I start making any PRs, I wanted to ask:

Do you currently have an i18n infrastructure set up for the docs (e.g., sphinx-intl), or a preferred way to handle translations?

Where would you prefer the translated files to be located within the repository?

Let me know if you are open to this and how I can best align with the project's workflow. Thanks!

comments.body:
👋 Thanks for opening your first issue here!

Please make sure you filled out the template with as much detail as possible. You might also want to take a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [code of conduct](https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/.github/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

¡Hola! @Silver19368 👋 Thanks for thinking about this! Always keen to spread PyGMT to more languages.

We haven't set up any sphinx internationalization plugin yet, the most we have currently is an external link to @andrebelem's tutorial in Portuguese at https://www.pygmt.org/v0.18.0/external_resources.html#tutorials. I will also mention @whyjz's comment at https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/770#issuecomment-805273966 that points to his https://github.com/whyjz/GMT-tutorials website that has a [weblate page](https://hosted.weblate.org/engage/gmt-tutorials/) which now includes 7 languages. That last one might be an easier entrypoint if you'd like to help translate just tutorials or the quickstart guide?

I'll also let other maintainers chime in, and tag @Esteban82 to see if there's other related resources around Latin America.

Hi @weiji14,

Thank you so much for the quick response!

I will definitely check out the Weblate link from @whyjz's repository. It sounds like an excellent and very accessible starting point for translating the tutorials.

I'll also wait to hear from @Esteban82, in case he has any additional comments or knows of other ongoing efforts in Latin America before I dive in.

Also, I'd love to know if there is any other way I can help with PyGMT tutorials or guides. When I first started using the library, the learning curve wasn't easy, but I owe a lot to this tool. I'm really motivated to actively contribute so that new users can understand it and get the most out of it.

Best regards,
Silver

Hi @Silver19368

Nothing to add from my side, but great to see you getting involved!

I'm not sure if it's still worth the time to translate documentation into other languages. Translation tools like Google Translate or DeepL have become more powerful in the AI age. Can we really do better than these tools?

> I'm not sure if it's still worth the time to translate documentation into other languages. Translation tools like Google Translate or DeepL have become more powerful in the AI age. Can we really do better than these tools?

I was actually also wondering about AI here. Translating the entire documentation is a huge task, and even more so keeping it up to date, considering changes to the codes, e.g., the new Alias system, parameter names for the modifiers, and high-level methods. I agree language barriers slow down the learning curve. Thus, I feel having tutorials in various languages can be helpful for beginners. They can be add to the ["External Resources"](https://www.pygmt.org/latest/external_resources.html) page, similar to andrebelem's tutorial in Portuguese.

I agree that with tools like Google Translate, translating all the documentation might not be the most efficient approach, especially considering the maintenance it involves. I could focus on getting back to adding examples to the code.
I'm closing the issue. Contributing examples are always welcome.

body: At https://www.pygmt.org/v0.19.0/install.html#testing-your-install we provide an example for users to test their installation, especially if semi-transparency works correctly. However, due to a bug in GMT 6.7.0 (xref: https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/gmt/issues/9125 and https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/gmt/pull/9126) semi-transparency is ignored for the `font` parameter of `Figure.text` (https://www.pygmt.org/dev/install.html#testing-your-install). I feel it makes sense to adjust the example in the PyGMT documentation to avoid confusion for users having GMT 6.7.0 installed, as even if they have installed a compatible Ghostscript version, the example indicates erroneously to them that there is an issue regarding semi-transparency related to Ghostscript.

title: Known issues in the PDF format of the PyGMT documentation
body:
This is the central issue to report/discuss the issues in the PDF format of the PyGMT documentation. The PDF file for the dev version (reflecting the main branch) is available at https://www.pygmt.org/dev/pygmt-docs.pdf.

- [x] On the first page, it say 'Author name not set'. It would be nice if we could grab the names from the CITATION.cff file somehow. [Set to "The PyGMT Developers" in PR #3840]

- [x] In the PDF file, the 'PyGMT Team' section lists everyone's profile pictures on 1 page (at a low-resolution). Unsure if there's a way to make those photos smaller. #4922

_Originally posted by @weiji14 in https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/pull/3765#pullrequestreview-2545575643_
         
- [x] Weird / confusing structure compared to the website. It looks like the sections of the README are used as chapter headings, and all sections on the website are listed under "Related topics", which is the last section of the README. [Fixed in #3840]

| website side bar | PDF contents |
| --- | --- |
| ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9a47dedf-a247-401c-9162-2178ac87a4e3) | ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fc26995d-672e-4b38-9b42-1db2e67a8779) |

- [x] The content of `README.md` is not included [See the reason in #3840] No longer an issue after we separated the README and the landing page #4746

comments.body:
>   [ ]  On the first page, it say 'Author name not set'. It would be nice if we could grab the names from the CITATION.cff file somehow.

Grabbing names from the CITATION.cff file means parsing the YAML file, which is extra coding efforts. In PR #3840, I have set the authors to `"The PyGMT Developers"` instead.

>   [ ]  Missing emojis, unsure if there's anyway to show them in LaTeX (if it involves downloading a large font file, we can skip it)
>   ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8d5abc20-2950-4c42-be9d-4ccbed37849a)

Currently, we type emojis directly into the text. It works well for HTML, but it doesn't work for LaTeX. If you check the TeX source files generated by `make pdf`, you will see that the raw emoji unicode characters are directly shown in the text. However, the LaTeX emoji package (https://ctan.math.washington.edu/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/emoji/emoji-doc.pdf
) expects a syntax like `\emoji{joy}` instead. A possible solution is [sphinxemoji](https://github.com/sphinx-contrib/emojicodes), but its syntax (`|:heart_eyes:|`) likely doesn't work in Markdown.

Actually, I'm thinking if we should remove the changelog section from the PDF documentation.

>   [ ]  In the PDF file, the 'PyGMT Team' section lists everyone's profile pictures on 1 page (at a low-resolution). Unsure if there's a way to make those photos smaller.

Related to upstream issue https://github.com/executablebooks/sphinx-design/issues/179. No solutions yet.

> * [ ]  Weird / confusing structure compared to the website. It looks like the sections of the README are used as chapter headings, and all sections on the website are listed under "Related topics", which is the last section of the README.
> 
> website side bar	PDF contents
> ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9a47dedf-a247-401c-9162-2178ac87a4e3)	![Image](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/94163266/420110563-fc26995d-672e-4b38-9b42-1db2e67a8779.png)

Yes, this is because we directly include the `README` file in the doc's `index.md` file:
https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/eb0ebe7b6fbd3fdc9b96ba663bdab7bab51371c1/doc/index.md?plain=1#L12-L16

I don't have a perfect solution yet, but PR #3840 fixes the PDF structure by excluding the `README` file from the PDF output.

title: Improve PyGMT documentation usability and consistency
body:
After redesigning the PyGMT documentation landing page and the project README (#4746), I feel it is a good time to further improve the documentation. Below are some documentation issues and ideas that we can discuss and address.

- [x] Improve version information shown in the footer. At the site footer, the dev version shows "Revision f8d331fd" and the release version shows "Revision v0.19.0". I think it would be clearer to show "Release 0.19.0" instead of "Revision v0.19.0" for release versions. #4920
- [x] Improve the ["Full installation"](https://www.pygmt.org/dev/install.html) page
  - [x] Add an introductory note at the beginning, for example: #4907
    > The "Quickstart" section provides the fastest way to install PyGMT, whereas the following sections provide more detailed, step-by-step instructions for users with different setups or those who want to install  the latest development version.
  - [x] List both required and optional dependencies (#4807).
- [x] Improve the ["PyGMT Ecosystem"](https://www.pygmt.org/dev/ecosystem.html) page #4911
  - [x] The page currently starts with "PyGMT provides a Python interface ...", which duplicates the Overview page. Since readers of this page likely already know what PyGMT is, this sentence could be removed.
  - [x] The PyGMT Ecosystem includes both dependencies of PyGMT and packages that depend on PyGMT. The current introduction only describes the former, so the wording should be updated.
  - [x] The ecosystem figure currently only shows PyGMT dependencies. Consider moving it to the "PyGMT dependencies" section.
  - [x] Add GMT as a PyGMT dependency.
  - [x] Currently, each package uses its name as a level-3 heading and includes the full official project description. Consider using [MyST definition lists](https://myst-parser.readthedocs.io/en/latest/syntax/typography.html#syntax-glossaries) with shorter descriptions to make the page more concise.
- [x] Redesign the ["Presentations"](https://www.pygmt.org/dev/presentations.html) page using the card layout (#4805).
- [x] Improve the ["Changelog"](https://www.pygmt.org/dev/changes.html) page. Contributors are currently listed using Markdown lists, which takes up significant vertical space, especially in the [PDF documentation](https://www.pygmt.org/dev/pygmt-docs.pdf)(~700 pages). Consider using a comma-separated list instead, e.g.,    `Author1, Author2, Author3`. #4906
- [x] Improve visibility of the PDF documentation. The PDF documentation has been available since v0.15.0 (#1606), although there are still some limitations (#3813). Currently, the dev PDF is available at https://www.pygmt.org/dev/pygmt-docs.pdf, and release PDFs are attached as release assets. Consider ways to make the PDF documentation easier to discover. commit 32fbfbc43d1e1630c224674589d03d0f3a15e104
- [x] Improve the ["PyGMT Team"](https://www.pygmt.org/dev/team.html) page. The page currently starts with four paragraphs of introductory text, which may be longer than necessary. Consider shortening it or moving some of the content into individual subsections. #4908

title: Add new exceptions for invalid inputs and deprecate GMTInvalidInput exception
body:
Currently, we have several exceptions defined in https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/blob/main/pygmt/exceptions.py.

Below is a simple command to count how often each exception is raised in the codebase (The `tests` directory and the `exceptions.py` file are excluded).
```bash
for e in \
    GMTError \
    GMTOSError \
    GMTCLibError \
    GMTCLibNotFoundError \
    GMTCLibNoSessionError \
    GMTVersionError \
    GMTInvalidInput \
    GMTImageComparisonFailure; 
do
    n=$(grep -R --exclude-dir=tests --exclude="exceptions.py" "raise $e" pygmt | wc -l)
    echo "$e: $n" 
done
```
the output is:
```
GMTError: 1
GMTOSError: 1
GMTCLibError: 16
GMTCLibNotFoundError: 1
GMTCLibNoSessionError: 1
GMTVersionError: 1
GMTInvalidInput: 87
GMTImageComparisonFailure: 1
```
Most exceptions are about the GMT C library, and is only used once or a few times. But the `GMTInvalidInput` exception is used 87 times and will definitely increase as we wrap more modules.

The `GMTInvalidInput` exception is general and doesn't tell exactly what's happening. I haven't checked the source codes carefully, but I feel the exceptions can be grouped into a few categories:

1. A required parameter is not given
2. Given parameters have conflicts 
3. A parameter is given with an incorrect type
4. A parameter is given with invalid values
5. Maybe more

I think we should have more accurate exceptions, e.g., 

- [x] `GMTParameterError`: for cases 1 and 2, maybe having more fine-grain exceptions like `GMTRequiredParameterError`/`GMTConflictParameterError`
- [x] `GMTTypeError`: for case 3, similar to the built-in `TypeError` #3999 
- [x] `GMTValueError`: for case 4, similar to the built-in `ValueError` #3985

The exception may even start with `PYGMT`, not `GMT`, since these are not directly related to GMT.

comments.body:
Does GMT C have different Error types or enum variants that we should try to match? I found https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/gmt/blob/1ed5e1bf4be46714e4124f9c1935e5bb14a6fb99/src/gmt_error_codes.h#L32, but unsure if there are some other ones. 

I'm thinking that at the `pygmt.clib` level, we should have thin wrappers to GMT C error enums, and then we can group those into higher level error types like `TypeError`, `ValueError`, etc as you've described.

> Does GMT C have different Error types or enum variants that we should try to match? I found https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/gmt/blob/1ed5e1bf4be46714e4124f9c1935e5bb14a6fb99/src/gmt_error_codes.h#L32, but unsure if there are some other ones.

These are all low-level error codes used in GMT's low-level APIs. When passing an incorrect value/type to a GMT module, GMT just returns the `GMT_PARSE_ERROR` error.

@Chuan1937 and I are working on the issue in PRs #4370 and #4003, but we're taking different approaches.

PR #4370 implements the `GMTRequiredParameterError`/`GMTConflictParameterError` exceptions, while PR #4003 implements the more general `GMTParameterError` exception

I prefer the general `GMTParameterError` exception, mainly because:

1. It's much shorter, so we don't have to wrap long lines when all the exceptions are imported. E.g.,
```
from pygmt.exceptions import GMTValueError, GMTParameterError, GMTTypeError
```
vs
```
from pygmt.exceptions import (
    GMTValueError,
    GMTTypeError,
    GMTRequiredParameterError,
    GMTConflictParameterError,
)
```
2. Consistent with the existing exceptions `GMTValueError`/`GMTTypeError`
3. More flexible. New parameter errors can be added without introducing new exception classes

What do @GenericMappingTools/pygmt-maintainers think?
I think stick with just a single `GMTParameterError`, but I do like @Chuan1937's clear messaging around conflicting parameters in #4370. Could maybe pull some aspects of that into #4003?

OK. Let's go with the single `GMTParameterError` exception. 

PR #4003 was opened to explore the possible types of errors related to parameters. From what I have learnt, the parameter errors can be grouped into the following categories:

1. One **or** a few parameters are required
2. At least one of the parameters *par1*, *par2*, *par3* is required
3. Only one of the parameters can be specified: *par1*, *par2*, *par3*
4. Parameter *par1* conflicts with *par2* [I feel it's same as catgeory 3]
5. Parameter *par1* conflicts with *par2*, *par3*, *par4*
6. Maybe more

In PR #4003, the error message for each category is:

1. `Required parameter(s) are missing: 'par1', 'par2', 'par3'.`
2. `At least one of the following parameters must be specified: 'par1', 'par2', 'par3'.`
3. `Mutually exclusive parameter(s) are specified: 'par1', 'par2'.`
4. Same as category 3
5. Not implemented yet

In PR #4370, the error messages look like:

1. `Missing required parameters: 'par1' and 'par2'.`
2. `Missing required parameters: 'par1' or 'par3'`.
3. `Conflicting parameters: 'par1' and 'par2'.`
4. Same as category 3
5. `Conflicting parameters: 'par1' and other parameters`

We should have clear and standardized error messages for each category. 

Please note that PR #4003 was opened for proof of concept. It contains too many changes and is difficult to review. I was planning to split it into smaller PRs, with each PR working on one specific type of parameter errors. I won't work on it in the following days, but I can review it. In other words, @Chuan1937, you can split PR #4003 into smaller PRs if you're interested.
Ok,I'll open some new PRs to slove it based on single exception `GMTParameterError`

Here is a summary table of the (preferred and alternative) parameter names and error message templates for each parameter error type. They're not final decisions and are open for comments and suggestions. | Error types | Preferred Parameter Name | Alternative Parameter Names | Error Message Template | | ---------------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Required** | `required` | `must_have`, `needed` | `Missing required parameter: '{param}'`
`Missing required parameters: '{a}', '{b}'` | | **At least one is required** | `at_least_one` | `need_one_of`, `any_of`, `one_of`, `required_any` | `Missing required parameters: '{a}', '{b}', '{c}'. Must specify at least one.`
`Must specify at least one of the parameters: '{a}', '{b}', '{c}'` | | ~~**Exactly one is required**~~ | ~~`exactly_one`~~ | ~~`mutually_exclusive`~~ | ~~`Mutually exclusive parameters: '{a}', '{b}', '{c}'. Specify exactly one.`~~ | | **At most one** | `at_most_one` | `mutually_exclusive` | `Mutually exclusive parameters: '{a}', '{b}', '{c}'. Specify at most one` | | **Conflicting** | `conflicts_with` | `conflicts`, `incompatible_with` | `Conflicting parameters: '{a}' cannot be used with '{b}', '{c}'` |

title: Improve the tutorial for Cartesian Histograms
body:
We already have a good tutorial for Cartesian Histograms at https://www.pygmt.org/0.19.0/tutorials/advanced/cartesian_histograms.html, which was initially developed more than 3 years ago (#2445).

Here are some ideas to improve the tutorial:

- The `series` parameter is one of the most important parameters that controls the histogram, but it's not explained well. The first subsection should focus on this parameter
- Inspired by [matplotlib's `hist` method's `histype` parameter](https://matplotlib.org/stable/api/_as_gen/matplotlib.pyplot.hist.html), I feel we should have a subsection showing different histogram styles, by different combinations of `fill`/`pen`/`stairs` (xref: https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/pull/4884#issue-5385364886). With this subsection, we could remove the existing "Stair-steps" subsection from the tutorial
- Horizontal histograms are less commonly used, so it makes little sense to have "Vertical and horizontal bars" at the start of the tutorial
- Maybe also add a subsection for adding the distribution curves

title: Pythonic implementation for the "series" parameter that accept xmin/xmax/inc and comma-separated sequence
body:
### Background

Many GMT modules use the same syntax to create a series of values. Examples include the `-T` option of [`histogram`](https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/6.7/histogram.html#t) and of `makecpt`. The syntax is:

```
-T[min/max/]inc[+b|n|u|...] | -Tfile | -Tval1,val2,val3,...
```

From the CLI, the option accepts four kinds of arguments:

- `min/max/inc` — three slash-separated values for *min*, *max*, and *inc*
- `inc` — a single increment value; *min* and *max* are usually inferred from the data or `-R`
- `val1,val2,val3,...` — a comma-separated list of values
- *file* — a file containing the values, one per line

## Proposa

Python users generally prefer to pass a list, tuple, or array instead of a hand-written string. For example, `bins=np.arange(0, 100, 10)` in matplotlib's `hist`. To accommodate this, PyGMT should accept the following inputs for `-T`:

| Input | Interpretation | Passed to GMT as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A single float | *inc* | `<inc>` |
| A string | Used verbatim; may be a file name, `min/max/inc`, or `val1,val2,...` | `<string>` |
| A tuple/list of length 3 | (*min*, *max*, *inc*) | `<min>/<max>/<inc>` |
| A tuple/list whose length is not 3 | A sequence of values | `<val1>,<val2>,<val3>,...` |
| Any other sequence (e.g. `range()`, `numpy.ndarray`, `pandas.Series`) | A sequence of values | `<val1>,<val2>,<val3>,...` |

### Caveats

- A tuple/list with exactly three values is ambiguous: `(-1000, 0, 100)` could mean either `-1000/0/100` or `-1000,0,100`. We define three-element tuples/lists as always being *min*/*max*/*inc* and we should document it clearly.
- `numpy.arange` excludes the stop value, whereas GMT's `-Tmin/max/inc` includes it. For example, `numpy.arange(1, 5, 1)` becomes `1,2,3,4`, while `-T1/5/1` means `1,2,3,4,5`.、
- `-T` option also supports many modifiers, e.g., `+b` for evenly spaced values in log2-domain. I feel these uses cases can be done by generating sequences using numpy, so I don't think we need to worry about Pythonic implementaitions of these modifiers. Anyway, users can always pass strings like `series="1/5/1+b"`.
 
### Implementation details
 
A comma-separated string becomes very long when the sequence contains many values or long floats (e.g. `0.1111111111`). GMT may crash if the resulting CLI string exceeds an internal length limit (I don't know the limits yet). To avoid the length limit, long sequences should be passed using the `-Tfile` syntax rather than inlined. Because GMT supports passing files through **virtual files**, this can be done without creating any temporary files on disk.

title: Migrate baseline images from DVC to Git LFS
body:
The baseline images in `pygmt/tests/baseline/*.png` have been tracked using DVC since PR #1036 (five years ago; the original idea came from https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/963#issuecomment-789277464). This setup has worked well, but it also has several drawbacks. I think it's time to consider whether we have a better solution.

## Drawbacks of DVC

- Requires installing `dvc`, which is unfamiliar to most contributors
- The workflow is relatively complicated: `dvc add`, `dvc push`, `git add`, and `git push` (xref: https://www.pygmt.org/v0.19.0/contributing.html#using-data-version-control-dvc-to-manage-test-images)
- Every maintainer needs to configure DVC locally
- Contributors must be added as collaborators on DagsHub before they can push DVC-tracked files
- Pulling DVC-tracked files now requires authentication (#4147)
- Several DVC-specific GitHub workflows are required to support the current setup

## Git LFS

[Git LFS](https://git-lfs.com/) is likely a better option for our use case. For files tracked by Git LFS, only small text pointer files are stored in the Git repository (similar to the current `*.dvc` files), while the actual file contents are stored separately. So updating baseline images won't increase the Git repository size.

Currently, PyGMT has ~240 baseline images with a total size of ~10 MB, which is well within GitHub LFS's free quota of 10 GB of storage and 10 GB of monthly bandwidth (xref: https://docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/git-lfs#free-use-of-git-lfs).

The setup is straightforward and only requires a few commands (see https://git-lfs.com/). Once configured, baseline images can be managed just like regular Git-tracked files using `git add`, `git pull`, and `git push`. This makes the workflow much more transparent and familiar for both maintainers and contributors.

Git LFS also integrates well with GitHub and pull requests. In my own fork, I have already migrated the baseline images to Git LFS on the main branch (https://github.com/seisman/pygmt). For example, if you visit https://github.com/seisman/pygmt/blob/main/pygmt/tests/baseline/test_basemap.png, GitHub displays the image directly, with a "Stored with Git LFS" note in the upper-left corner. When a baseline image is updated in a pull request, GitHub can also display image diffs directly (see https://github.com/seisman/pygmt/pull/4/changes for an example).

Overall, I think Git LFS satisfies our requirements while providing a simpler and more contributor-friendly workflow than DVC.

## TODO

- [x] Discuss whether to migrate from DVC to Git LFS
- [x] Migrate `pygmt/tests/baseline/*.png` from DVC to Git LFS
- [x] Remove `dvc` from `environment.yml`
- [x] Remove `.dvc/` and `.dvcignore`
- [x] Update `MANIFEST.in`
- [x] Update the Maintainers' Guide
- [x] Update the Contributors' Guide
- [x] Remove the `dvc-diff.yml` workflow, because GitHub can display diffs for LFS-tracked images directly in the web UI
- [x] Remove the `cache_dvc.yaml` workflow, which was added as a workaround for #4147
- [x] Update the `style_checks.yaml` workflow
- [x] Update the `ci_tests.yaml` workflow
- [x] Update the `ci_tests_dev.yaml` workflow
- [x] Update the `release-baseline-image.yml` workflow
- [x] Ensure that source and binary distributions do not include the baseline images
- [x] Remove DAGsHUB secrets from GitHub settings
- [ ] Decide if we want to delete the DagsHub repo https://dagshub.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt, which is needed for old versions
- [ ] Explore if a similar migration make sense to the GMT repository

I have to admit that I’ve never used Git LFS before, so I’d especially like to hear from @weiji14, who implemented the DVC mechanism in PR #1036 and may have more experience with both DVC and Git LFS. I’m also pinging @GenericMappingTools/pygmt-maintainers for comments and feedback.

comments.body: Here is a GMT CLI script to understand the behavior of the `-G` option: ``` gmt begin image-G gmt basemap -R0/10/0/5 -JX10c/5c -Baf -B+glightblue gmt image @vader1.png -Dx0/0 gmt image @vader1.png -Dx1/0 -G gmt image @vader1.png -Dx2/0 -Gblue gmt image @vader1.png -Dx1/1 -G+f gmt image @vader1.png -Dx2/1 -Gblue+f gmt image @vader1.png -Dx1/2 -G+b gmt image @vader1.png -Dx2/2 -Gblue+b # Error: Only one of fore/back-ground can be transparent for 1-bit images gmt image @vader1.png -Dx0/3 -G+b -G+f gmt image @vader1.png -Dx1/3 -Gblue+b -Gred+f # Your -G+t is ignored for 1-bit images; see +b/+f modifiers instead gmt image @vader1.png -Dx0/4 -Gblack+t gmt end show ``` As shown above, `-G` without modifiers applies to the foreground color by default. Currently, we use the parameter name `bitcolor` (or `bit_color`) but the argument is not Pythonic. I think it makes more sense to split it into multiple parameters, e.g., `bgcolor`/`fgcolor` (note that the same names are used in the [`Pattern`](https://www.pygmt.org/dev/api/generated/pygmt.params.Pattern.html#pygmt.params.Pattern.bgcolor) class). - `-G`/`-G+f` => `fgcolor=""` - `-Gblue`/`-Gblue+f` => `fgcolor="blue"` - `-G+b` => `bgcolor=""` - `-Gblue+b` => `bgcolor=""` - `-Gblue+b -Gred+f` => `bgcolor="blue", fgcolor="red"` The `+t` modifier is different, and only works for colored images. ~~What about `transparent_colors`, which can takes a single color or a list of colors.~~ Edit: `-t` only accepts only color and can't be repeated, so `transparent_color` make more sense.

title: Figure.hlines/Figure.vlines: Plot horizontal/vertical lines
body:
*This issue serves as the central place for discussing and tracking the implementation of the `hlines` and `vlines` methods in PyGMT. The issue will be closed when the initial implementation is complete. Progress is tracked at https://github.com/orgs/GenericMappingTools/projects/3.*

## Documentation

- GMT: https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/dev/plot.html
- PyGMT `hlines`: https://www.pygmt.org/dev/api/generated/pygmt.Figure.hlines.html
- PyGMT `vlines`: https://www.pygmt.org/dev/api/generated/pygmt.Figure.vlines.html

## Parameters

☑️: *Implemented*; ⬜: *To be implemented/discussed*; ~~Strikethrough~~: *Won't implement*.

`Figure.hlines` and `Figure.vlines` are high-level PyGMT wrappers around `Figure.plot` (which internally uses GMT's `plot` module). They expose the following subset of `Figure.plot` parameters:

- [ ] `-B`: `frame`
- [ ] `-J`: `projection`
- [x] `-N`: `no_clip`
- [ ] `-R`: `region`
- [ ] ~~`-U`~~: Use `Figure.timestamp` instead.
- [ ] `-V`: `verbose`
- [x] `-W`: `pen`
- [ ] ~~`-X`/`-Y`~~: Use `Figure.shift_origin` instead.
- [x] `-c`: `panel` #4892
- [x] `-l`: `label`
- [x] `-p`: `perspective`
- [ ] `-t`: `transparency`
- [ ] ~~`--PAR=value`~~: Use `pygmt.config` instead.

## Notes

`Figure.hlines` plots horizontal lines at specified Y-coordinates; `Figure.vlines` plots vertical lines at specified X-coordinates. Both methods internally call `Figure.plot` with `straight_line="x"` or `straight_line="y"` respectively, and resample to at least 4 points to support geographic/polar projections.

The term "horizontal"/"vertical" differs by coordinate system:
- **Cartesian**: straight lines
- **Polar**: arcs along constant radius / straight lines along constant azimuth
- **Geographic**: arcs along parallels (constant latitude) / meridians (constant longitude)

- [x] Add a tutorial or gallery example

- #2797 — higher-level plotting methods discussion

comments.body:
For a colorbar, the annotations and labels can be set by either the [`-B`](https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/dev/gmt.html#b-full) option (can't be used with `-L`) or the `-S` option (a simplified version of the `-B` option). 

The `-B` option is one of the most complicated GMT options, but most `-B` settings do not affect the colorbar. For example, `-BWSEN+tTITLE` doesn't work. As far as I can see, the `-B` syntax that has an effect for a colorbar is

**-Bx**_intervals_[**+a**_angle_][**+l**_label_][**+p**_prefix_][**+u**_unit_]
**-By+l**_label_

Here, the x-axis and y-axis represent the long and short dimensions, respectively, so the y-axis only has a label. One common use case is `-Bxa10f5+l"Focal Depth" -By+l"km"`. 

The current PyGMT syntax is `frame=["xa10f5+lFocal Depth", "y+lkm"]`. After the implementation of the `Frame`/`Axis` classes (PR #4406), it will be
```
frame=Frame(xaxis=Axis(annot=10, tick=5, label="Focal Depth"), yaxis=Axis(label="km")
```
However, it still appears complicated and imperfect. What about splitting it into separate parameters

- `xlabel`/`ylabel` (`colorbar` docs calls them `label`/`unit`): labels for x- and y-axis
- `annot`, `tick`, `grid`: intervals for the annotations, ticks and grids
- `angle`/`prefix`/`unit` or `annot_angle`/`annot_prefix`/`annot_unit`(or `annot_suffix`) for controlling the annotations.

The new syntax would be `annot=10, tick=5, xlabel="Focal Depth", ylabel="km"`. Internally, we need to convert these parameters into the `Frame`/`Axis` class and pass it to the `frame` parameter.

Here is a comparison between different versions:
| Version | Example |
|---|---|
| GMT | `-Bxa10+l"Focal Depth" -By+l"km"` |
| PyGMT v0.18.0 | `frame=["xa10f5+lFocal Depth", "y+lkm"]` |
| After PR #4406 | `frame=Frame(xaxis=Axis(annot=10, tick=5, label="Focal Depth"), yaxis=Axis(label="km")`|
| The new implemention | `annot=10, tick=5, xlabel="Focal Depth", ylabel="km"` |

As mentioned above, the `-S` option is a simplified version of the `-B` option, which can work when the `-L` option is used. Its syntax is like **-S**[**+a**_angle_][**+c**|**n**][**+r**][**+s**][**+x**_label_][**+y**_unit_]. It can also set the annotation angle, x-label, and y-label (it's called *unit* in GMT ~~but I think it's a mistake~~). So the option can also be split into multiple parameters, e.g., `annot_angle`, `annot_custom`, `annot_numerical`, `annot_minmax`, `no_gridlines`, `label`, `unit`. We can decide if `annot_angle`/`label`/`unit` should be converted to `-B` or `-S`, depending on if `-L` is used.

Something to think about: Whether to add an option in `Figure.colorbar` to plot a circular colorbar based on some examples in https://github.com/GenericMappingTools/pygmt/issues/3638. (we can continue discussing in #3638 since this issue is closed).

Trying to implement a Pythonic API for the `-L` and `-Z` option. ## `-L` option The script below tries to understand the behavior of different `-L` options for four types of CPTs: (top left): continuous CPT; (top right): discrete CPT; (bottom left): discrete CPT with unequal z-interval; (bottom right): categorical CPT: ``` gmt begin colorbar_L png gmt basemap -R0/16/0/10 -Jx1c -Baf gmt makecpt -Cseis -T0/100 gmt colorbar -C -Dx1/1+w8c gmt colorbar -C -Dx4/1+w8c -L0.2 gmt colorbar -C -Dx7/1+w8c -Li gmt colorbar -C -Dx10/1+w8c -LI gmt colorbar -C -Dx13/1+w8c -Li0.2 gmt basemap -R0/11/0/10 -Jx1c -Baf -X17c gmt makecpt -Cseis -T0/100/11 gmt colorbar -C -Dx1/1+w8c gmt colorbar -C -Dx3/1+w8c -L0.2 gmt colorbar -C -Dx5/1+w8c -Li gmt colorbar -C -Dx7/1+w8c -LI gmt colorbar -C -Dx9/1+w8c -Li0.2 gmt basemap -R0/11/0/10 -Jx1c -Baf -X-17c -Y-11c gmt makecpt -Cseis -T0,10,30,60,100 gmt colorbar -C -Dx1/1+w8c gmt colorbar -C -Dx3/1+w8c -L0.2 gmt colorbar -C -Dx5/1+w8c -Li gmt colorbar -C -Dx7/1+w8c -LI gmt colorbar -C -Dx9/1+w8c -Li0.2 gmt basemap -R0/11/0/10 -Jx1c -Baf -X12c gmt makecpt -Ccategorical -T0,10,30,60,100 gmt colorbar -C -Dx1/1+w8c gmt colorbar -C -Dx3/1+w8c -L0.2 gmt colorbar -C -Dx5/1+w8c -Li gmt colorbar -C -Dx7/1+w8c -LI gmt colorbar -C -Dx9/1+w8c -Li0.2 gmt end show ``` In summary: - `-L`: Force equal-sized color rectangles - `-L0.2`: Controls the gaps between color rectangles. Default is 0 for most CPT, but is non-zero for categorical CPT. - `-Li`: annote color rectangles by intervals (default use the lower range) - `-LI`: same as `-Li`, but include background and foreground values in annotations ## `-Z` option The `-Z` option can control the width of color rectangles. I've created a sample `widthfile` with content: ``` 0.25 0.35 0.45 0.55 0.55 0.65 0.75 0.85 0.95 ``` then adding `-Zwidthfile` and re-run the script above (please ignore a few warnings): ## Proposed API I feel `-L` and `-Z` can be implemented as three parameters - `rectangle_widths`: it can be `"equal"` (i.e., `-L`), or accept a sequence of widths for different rectangles (more Pythonic than passing a width file) - `rectangle_gap`: the gap (i.e., `-L0.2`) - `annot_style`: can be `None` (GMT's default value), `"interval"` (`-Li`, annot using intervals e.g., `10-20`), and `"interval_with_bg_fg"` (`-LI`) Let me know if you have comments before I try to implement it.

GMT 6.7.0 has just been released and introduces [**-H** for `colorbar`](https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/6.7/colorbar.html#h) to not have the automatic scaling of the colorbar font size based on the colorbar width applied:

> From GMT 6.5 on, colorbar annotation fonts are auto-scaled. Use this option to prevent that effect and let user set fonts as they wish.

Maybe this can be helpful and can reduce the confusion. Will need to test this and think about adding an alias for **-H**. Also need to update the note in the docs https://www.pygmt.org/dev/api/generated/pygmt.Figure.colorbar.html#pygmt.Figure.colorbar.

title: Figure.psconvert: Convert [E]PS file(s) to other formats using Ghostscript
body:
This issue serves as the central place for discussing and tracking the implementation of the `Figure.psconvert` method in PyGMT. The issue will be closed when the initial implementation is complete. Progress is tracked at https://github.com/orgs/GenericMappingTools/projects/3.

## Documentation

- GMT: https://docs.generic-mapping-tools.org/dev/psconvert.html
- GMT.jl: https://www.generic-mapping-tools.org/GMTjl_doc/documentation/modules/psconvert
- PyGMT: https://www.pygmt.org/dev/api/generated/pygmt.Figure.psconvert.html

## GMT Option Flags and Modifiers

☑️: *Implemented*; ⬜: *To be implemented/discussed*; ~~Strikethrough~~: *Won't implement*.

- [ ] `<psfiles>`
- [ ] `-A[+r][+u]`
- [x] `-C`: `gs_option`
- [ ] `-D<dir>`
- [x] `-E`: `dpi`
- [x] `-F`: `prefix`
- [x] `-G`: `gs_path`
- [ ] `-H<scale>`
- [ ] `-I[+m<margins>][+s[m]<width>[/<height>]][+S<scale>]]`
- [ ] `-L<list>`
- [ ] `-Mb|f<psfile>`
- [ ] `-N[+f<fade>][+g<backfill>][+k<fadefill>][+p[<pen>]]]`
- [ ] `-P`
- [ ] `-Q[g|p|t]1|2|4]`
- [ ] `-S`
- [ ] `-Tb|e|E|f|F|g|G|j|m|s|t[+m][+q<quality>]]`
- [x] `-V`: `verbose`
- [ ] `-W[+a<mode>[<alt>]][+c][+f<minfade>/<maxfade>][+g][+k][+l<lodmin>/<lodmax>][+n<name>][+o<folder>][+t<title>][+u<URL>]]`
- [ ] `-Z`
- [ ] `-!`
- [ ] ~~`--PAR=<value>`~~: Use `pygmt.config` instead.

## Notes on Input Formats

- `Figure.psconvert` is a method on `pygmt.Figure`; it converts the active figure's internal PostScript to the requested format using Ghostscript.
- If no active figure exists, an error is raised.
- The `prefix` parameter must be a non-empty string pointing to an existing directory; the method raises `FileNotFoundError` if the parent directory does not exist.
- The output format is determined by `fmt` (`-T`); multiple formats can be combined (e.g., `fmt="ef"` produces both EPS and PDF).
- `crop=True` (default) trims whitespace around the figure; append `"+u"` to also strip the GMT timestamp.

## Linked Pull Requests

- [x] Initial feature implementation – #31
- [x] Move `Figure.psconvert` to a separate file – #3553
- [x] Add `resize` (`-I`) parameter – #2406
- [x] Add `bb_style` (`-N`) parameter – #3233
- [ ] Implement `-D` (`directory`) option to set the output directory
- [ ] Implement `-L` (`list`) option for batch conversion of multiple files
- [ ] Implement `-W` (`world_file`) option for GIS-compatible raster output

## Related Issues and Discussions

- `Figure.psconvert` is called implicitly by `Figure.savefig`; users who need more control over Ghostscript options should call `Figure.psconvert` directly.
- The `anti_aliasing` parameter (`-Q`) is useful when producing raster images for presentations or publications at lower DPI settings.
- The `-L` (file list) and `-Tf` (multi-page PDF) combination is the standard GMT approach for assembling a series of figures into a single PDF document.
